---
title: "Replication Paper: Ghost Games: Crowds, Referee Bias, and Home Advantage in European Football Leagues"
date: "18/07/2025"
author: "Riccardo Gaist"
output: html_document
---

**Abstract**

This paper replicates a prior study on the influence of fans on home field advantage in European first division football, utilizing a five-year data set from the 2020 English, Spanish, Italian, and German leagues, including crowd-less games. Through multivariate regression analysis, we confirm the original finding that referees, when crowds are present, award fewer fouls and cards but more penalty kicks to the home team. The elimination of fans is also re-confirmed to remove these biases in referee decisions. While replicating most of the original analysis, this study omits the original Table 4 due to data constraints. New contributions include a graphical analysis identifying the strongest determinants of goal difference. Furthermore, a sub sample regression on teams with low elo difference reveals that for these teams, an increase in elo difference has a substantial impact on goal differential, a finding not explored in the original work. Overall, our findings corroborate the significant but nuanced influence of crowds on referee judgment, while highlighting that the majority of home advantage persists independently of fan presence.

**Introduction**

The home advantage in football has long been recognized as a consistent and measurable phenomenon. Across numerous leagues and competitions, empirical studies have demonstrated that teams tend to perform better when playing on their home ground. Outcomes such as goals scored, points earned, and win probability systematically favor the home side. One of the most frequently cited explanations for this advantage is the presence of a supportive and vocal crowd, which is believed to enhance player performance and influence referee behavior. However, identifying the causal effect of crowd presence has traditionally been difficult, primarily due to the lack of exogenous variation in attendance conditions.

The COVID-19 pandemic presented a unique natural experiment. In the final stages of the 2019–2020 season, matches across Europe were played in empty stadiums due to public health restrictions. This sudden and widespread removal of fans allowed researchers to isolate and examine the influence of crowds on match dynamics and officiating decisions. In their original study, Reade, Schreyer, and Singleton (2022) used this context to show that referees became less biased in favor of home teams when spectators were absent. Their findings suggest that the home advantage—especially in terms of foul calls, yellow cards, red cards, and penalty awards—was significantly reduced in so-called ghost games.

This paper replicates and extends their analysis using the same dataset, but re-implements the procedures entirely in R. The replication focuses on matches played during the 2019 season, including both pre-pandemic and ghost games. This restricted and temporally coherent sample provides a clear empirical setting for evaluating the original hypotheses. Replicating established results using independent tools and frameworks strengthens the transparency and credibility of empirical research. This study aims to verify the robustness of the original findings while remaining faithful to their structure and theoretical motivation.

In addition to reproducing the main statistical models, the paper introduces several extensions. It includes robustness checks on subsamples of the data, such as matches involving teams with similar Elo ratings and those played with Video Assistant Referee (VAR) technology in place. These tests assess whether the estimated effects are consistent across different competitive and institutional contexts. Moreover, this study contributes a graphical analysis that identifies the strongest predictors of goal difference. This visualization offers an intuitive understanding of how referee decisions and team characteristics shape match outcomes, complementing the regression-based approach used in the original paper.

Overall, the replication confirms the central finding that crowd presence significantly influences referee behavior and, by extension, competitive balance in football. At the same time, it underscores the value of replication studies for ensuring that empirical claims are both reliable and generalizable.

This work contributes to broader academic debates on behavioral biases in officiating and the structural determinants of fairness and performance in professional sport. By examining how the absence of spectators affects key decisions made by referees, the study engages with a growing literature on the psychological and contextual influences that shape judgment in high-stakes environments. It highlights the vulnerability of decision-makers to subtle forms of social pressure, even in domains that are formally governed by rules and institutional oversight. Furthermore, the findings provide empirical support for the argument that sporting outcomes are not determined solely by team performance but are also conditioned by situational factors that affect how the game is interpreted and regulated. In doing so, the study contributes not only to the field of sports economics but also to interdisciplinary discussions on the role of accountability, cognitive bias, and institutional design in maintaining competitive integrity.

**Literature Review**

The existence of a home advantage has been widely documented across a variety of sports disciplines. Gomez, Pollard, and Luiz-Pascual (2011), for instance, examined nine different sports in Spain and found that home teams enjoyed a statistically significant advantage in all of them. Similarly, Jamieson (2010), through a meta-analysis covering ten sports, estimated that home teams win approximately 60% of matches on average. However, the magnitude of the advantage varies across sports: football, basketball, and rugby exhibit the most substantial home advantages, while sports such as baseball, golf, and cricket show comparatively weaker effects. In the context of European football specifically, Leite (2017) reported that teams in the top ten leagues secured roughly 58% of their total points when playing at home.

More recent estimates suggest a decline in the strength of the home advantage in football. This observation aligns with earlier findings by Pollard (1986) and Smith (2003), who identified a long-term downward trend in home advantage across several leagues. Among the explanatory mechanisms proposed in the literature, greater familiarity with the pitch, travel-related fatigue for the visiting team, and the psychological influence of the home crowd on both players and referees are commonly cited (Pollard & Pollard, 2005).

Importantly, the influence of crowd presence on referee decision-making has been examined through both empirical and experimental approaches. Nevill, Balmer, and Williams (2002) provided controlled evidence that exposure to crowd noise can significantly alter referees' judgments in favor of home teams, suggesting that auditory cues may unconsciously bias officiating. This line of research complements observational studies that document a reduction in referee bias when crowds are absent, reinforcing the view that home advantage is partly socially constructed through environmental pressures.
